Or digoxin 125–250 mcg OD (if contraindication to beta-blocker; elderly; HFrEF)
Or rate-limiting calcium blocker: diltiazem 60 mg TDS (if no HF)
RHYTHM CONTROL (selected: younger, symptomatic, recent onset <12 months, HF):
Electrical cardioversion (DCCV) after 4+ weeks anticoagulation (or TOE to exclude LA thrombus)

[WARNING] VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery (NG89, 2018). Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after surgery if bleeding risk allows, for at least 7 days.

Electrophysiology (Routine): Ablation consideration for symptomatic AF refractory to antiarrhythmics

Draft: SOAP Note — Working diagnosis: Chronic Kidney Disease (Stage 3–5) (P=99%) — auto-populate from collected history and exam.
IDENTIFY & TREAT CAUSE:
PRERENAL (commonest — dehydration, sepsis, cardiac output): IV fluid challenge; treat sepsis
INTRINSIC (ATN, nephritis, drugs): stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion)

POSTRENAL (obstruction): urgent renal USS → nephrostomy/stent if hydronephrosis; obstructed infected or solitary kidney → emergency decompression (EAU 2024); bladder outflow obstruction → urethral catheter, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (hourly urine output, replace losses); avoid NSAIDs in AKI
Stop / withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and metformin during AKI; restart when renal function recovers (NICE NG148); urinalysis (dipstick) for every patient with AKI
FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, high-output stoma): volume replacement — 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus → reassess response (JVP, UO, BP)
Oliguric AKI (UO <0.5 mL/kg/h): assess volume status; diuretics only for fluid overload, not to treat AKI (NICE NG148)
Fluid overload: fluid restrict ± furosemide; consider dialysis
HYPERKALAEMIA MANAGEMENT:
K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL) — cardioprotection (UK Kidney Association 2023)
Insulin–glucose: 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose IV; monitor capillary glucose for 12 h (UKKA 2023)
⚠ K⁺ 6.2 mmol/L: nebulised salbutamol withheld — an adjunct for severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.5 mmol/L) only (UKKA 2023).
Kayexalate / patiromer / sodium zirconium (GI elimination)
Restrict dietary K⁺; stop K⁺-sparing drugs
RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) — indications:
Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 despite treatment)
Refractory acidosis (pH <7.1)
Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis
DRUG DOSING: adjust all renally-cleared drugs; check BNF

INTRINSIC (ATN, nephritis, drugs): stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion)

FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, high-output stoma): volume replacement — 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus → reassess response (JVP, UO, BP)
Oliguric AKI (UO <0.5 mL/kg/h): assess volume status; diuretics only for fluid overload, not to treat AKI (NICE NG148)
Fluid overload: fluid restrict ± furosemide; consider dialysis

K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL) — cardioprotection (UK Kidney Association 2023)
⚠ K⁺ 5.4 mmol/L: potassium-shifting treatment withheld — it is for K⁺ ≥ 6.0 mmol/L (UKKA 2023); treat the cause and repeat K⁺.
⚠ K⁺ 5.4 mmol/L: nebulised salbutamol withheld — an adjunct for severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.5 mmol/L) only (UKKA 2023).

Restrict dietary K⁺; stop K⁺-sparing drugs
RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) — indications:
Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 despite treatment)

Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis

expectations.note: USPSTF 2021 / ACG 2021: average-risk screening from 45. ACG 2021: one FDR with CRC diagnosed < 60 (father at 58) → colonoscopy from age 40 (or 10 years before the relative’s age at diagnosis), repeated every 5 years — so he is overdue on the ACG reading. BSG 2020 (UK) would not add colonoscopic surveillance for a single FDR diagnosed ≥ 50. The practice’s policy needs the surgeon’s decision. Not observable in the web harness: the dashboard feeds the Family History field (ClinicalPromptsStrip familyHistory) to computeClinicalPrompts, but the vignette schema has no family-history input, so web-runner passes []. In the dashboard the "FHx colorectal cancer, age 35–49" prompt would probably add a colonoscopy. Needs a familyHistory input in the schema and both runners. Without a family history there is no screening prompt before 50: the average-risk "colorectal_screen" prompt starts at age 50 (USPSTF 2021 and ACG 2021: 45) and offers FOBT every 2 years rather than annual FIT. Web, 2026-09-25 (fix-web-screening): now observed in the harness — the preventive-screening engine reads the "Family history: …" and "Lynch syndrome" comorbidity entries, which the dashboard passes too; web removed from unverified.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Act Now: Sepsis — Initiate 1-Hour Bundle — Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics; IV antibiotics within 1 hour if suspected infection (broad-spectrum; narrow when cultures return); IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 h if lactate ≥4 or hypotension; Vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP <65 despite resuscitation; Measure serum lactate; repeat if initial ≥2 mmol/L; Identify and control source (imaging ± surgical intervention)
Repeat lactate in 2 h — Lactate ≥2 — clearance target ≥10% per hour in sepsis resuscitation.
IMMEDIATE RESUSCITATION (Sepsis Six within 1 hour):
O₂ (target SpO₂ >94%)
IV access × 2 + blood cultures before antibiotics
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics: tazobactam/piperacillin 4.5g 8-hourly + metronidazole 500mg TDS
IV fluid resuscitation: 500 mL crystalloid bolus → reassess
Urinary catheter — strict fluid balance
Serial lactate
NBM + NG tube on free drainage
Analgesia: IV morphine (do not withhold)
Urgent surgical review
OPERATIVE MANAGEMENT (most require surgery):
PERFORATED PU:
Laparoscopic washout + omental patch (Graham's patch)
Open repair if laparoscopy contraindicated / contamination heavy
COLONIC PERFORATION:
Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid — most common) or primary anastomosis if fit + low contamination
POST-OPERATIVE: proton pump inhibitor IV → oral; H. pylori eradication (PU)
NON-OPERATIVE (sealed perforation — CT confirmed, stable, low CRP):
Selected cases: IV antibiotics + strict monitoring + CT at 48h
Surgery if any deterioration
PATIENT-SPECIFIC SAFETY CHECKS (review before acting):

[WARNING] Insulin-treated diabetes: continue basal (long-acting) insulin — never omit it; give 80% of the usual dose the evening before and on the day; variable-rate IV insulin if more than one meal will be missed; capillary glucose and ketone monitoring; first on the list where possible (CPOC 2021).

[WARNING] VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery (NG89, 2018). Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after surgery if bleeding risk allows, for at least 7 days.

[WARNING] Emergency laparotomy / high-risk surgery: document the predicted mortality risk pre-operatively (NELA risk calculator or P-POSSUM); if ≥ 5%, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present and planned post-operative critical care (NELA; RCS 2018 The Higher Risk General Surgical Patient). Age ≥ 65 or frail: elderly-medicine (geriatric) review.
[INFO] Metformin: continue if only one meal is missed; omit if more than one meal will be missed, eGFR < 60 mL/min or IV contrast is planned (CPOC 2021).

management.text: Urgent (< 4 h): Small Bowel Obstruction — Lactate 2.4 mmol/L: Tissue hypoperfusion — goal-directed IV fluid resuscitation, reassess in 2 h; IV access + Hartmann's 1–2 L over 2–4 h (bowel obstruction causes significant third-space loss); Analgesia: morphine IV (reassess regularly); Anti-emetic: metoclopramide or ondansetron IV; NG tube (nasogastric decompression): wide-bore, free drainage + aspirate every hour; IDC for urine output monitoring; Nil by mouth
Repeat lactate in 2 h — Lactate ≥2 — clearance target ≥10% per hour in sepsis resuscitation.
Schedule: Small Bowel Obstruction — Required within 4 hours — HDU / Step-down.
IMMEDIATE:
NBM; IV access × 2; urinary catheter (fluid balance)
IV crystalloid resuscitation: 0.9% NaCl or Hartmann's
Nasogastric tube (NG) on free drainage — decompress + reduce vomiting
IV antiemetic: ondansetron 8 mg or metoclopramide 10 mg
Analgesia: IV morphine 2.5–5 mg titrated (do not withhold — does not mask signs)
Electrolyte replacement (K⁺ particularly)
CONSERVATIVE TRIAL (adhesion SBO, no signs of strangulation):
48–72h NG decompression + IV fluids; serial clinical examination
Water-soluble contrast study (Gastrografin) at 24 h — therapeutic + diagnostic; adhesive SBO without strangulation only — not for a hernia, closed-loop or strangulated obstruction (WSES/Bologna 2017)
80% adhesion SBO resolves conservatively
OPERATIVE INDICATIONS:
Strangulation (peritonism, fever, leucocytosis, lactate rise, blood supply)
Complete obstruction failing conservative × 48–72h
Hernia (external) causing obstruction → emergency surgery (hernia repair ± bowel resection); do not attempt reduction if strangulation is suspected (WSES 2017)
Tumour / volvulus / intussusception → surgery
Surgical options: adhesiolysis, hernia repair, resection ± anastomosis
Broad-spectrum antibiotics if operative: co-amoxiclav 1.2g IV or cefuroxime + metronidazole

[WARNING] Frailty / delirium risk (age 86, age 86): delirium prevention and 4AT screening (NICE CG103); comprehensive geriatric assessment and elderly-medicine (geriatric) input; shared decision-making with goals of care and a treatment-escalation plan documented (CPOC 2021 perioperative care for people living with frailty).

[WARNING] Emergency laparotomy / high-risk surgery: document the predicted mortality risk pre-operatively (NELA risk calculator or P-POSSUM); if ≥ 5%, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present and planned post-operative critical care (NELA; RCS 2018 The Higher Risk General Surgical Patient). Emergency Department (Emergency): Admit for fluid resuscitation + NG decompression
Follow-up at 2–6 weeks post-operatively. Bowel function review. Recurrence counselling.

management.text: Calculate: NEWS2 — National Early Warning Score 2 — standardised track-and-trigger for physiological deterioration.
Draft: SOAP Note — Working diagnosis: Acute Kidney Injury (P=39%) — auto-populate from collected history and exam.
IDENTIFY & TREAT CAUSE:
PRERENAL (commonest — dehydration, sepsis, cardiac output): IV fluid challenge; treat sepsis
INTRINSIC (ATN, nephritis, drugs): stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion)

POSTRENAL (obstruction): urgent renal USS → nephrostomy/stent if hydronephrosis; obstructed infected or solitary kidney → emergency decompression (EAU 2024); bladder outflow obstruction → urethral catheter, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (hourly urine output, replace losses); avoid NSAIDs in AKI
Stop / withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and metformin during AKI; restart when renal function recovers (NICE NG148); urinalysis (dipstick) for every patient with AKI
FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, high-output stoma): volume replacement — 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus → reassess response (JVP, UO, BP)
Oliguric AKI (UO <0.5 mL/kg/h): assess volume status; diuretics only for fluid overload, not to treat AKI (NICE NG148)
Fluid overload: fluid restrict ± furosemide; consider dialysis
HYPERKALAEMIA MANAGEMENT:
K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL) — cardioprotection (UK Kidney Association 2023)
Insulin–glucose: 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose IV; monitor capillary glucose for 12 h (UKKA 2023)
Salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised (K⁺ shift)
Kayexalate / patiromer / sodium zirconium (GI elimination)
Restrict dietary K⁺; stop K⁺-sparing drugs
RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) — indications:
Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 despite treatment)
Refractory acidosis (pH <7.1)
Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis
DRUG DOSING: adjust all renally-cleared drugs; check BNF
Nephrology (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI stage 2/3 — specialist nephrology input — Intrinsic AKI (e.g. glomerulonephritis) → urgent biopsy consideration
Urology (Urgent (2 wk)): Obstructive AKI — urgent decompression (DJ stent / nephrostomy)
Intensive Care (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI with haemodynamic compromise or hyperkalaemia refractory to medical management → RRT
Nephrology review if no recovery at 48–72h. Repeat U&E at 48h, then weekly until creatinine stable. Avoid nephrotoxins long-term.
Review within 24–48 hours.

IDENTIFY & TREAT CAUSE:
PRERENAL (commonest — dehydration, sepsis, cardiac output): IV fluid challenge; treat sepsis
INTRINSIC (ATN, nephritis, drugs): stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion)

POSTRENAL (obstruction): urgent renal USS → nephrostomy/stent if hydronephrosis; obstructed infected or solitary kidney → emergency decompression (EAU 2024); bladder outflow obstruction → urethral catheter, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (hourly urine output, replace losses); avoid NSAIDs in AKI
Stop / withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and metformin during AKI; restart when renal function recovers (NICE NG148); urinalysis (dipstick) for every patient with AKI
FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, high-output stoma): volume replacement — 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus → reassess response (JVP, UO, BP)
Oliguric AKI (UO <0.5 mL/kg/h): assess volume status; diuretics only for fluid overload, not to treat AKI (NICE NG148)
Fluid overload: fluid restrict ± furosemide; consider dialysis
HYPERKALAEMIA MANAGEMENT:
K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL) — cardioprotection (UK Kidney Association 2023)
⚠ K⁺ 3.3 mmol/L: potassium-shifting treatment withheld — it is for K⁺ ≥ 6.0 mmol/L (UKKA 2023); treat the cause and repeat K⁺.
⚠ K⁺ 3.3 mmol/L: nebulised salbutamol withheld — an adjunct for severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.5 mmol/L) only (UKKA 2023).
Kayexalate / patiromer / sodium zirconium (GI elimination)
Restrict dietary K⁺; stop K⁺-sparing drugs
RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) — indications:
Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 despite treatment)
Refractory acidosis (pH <7.1)
Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis
DRUG DOSING: adjust all renally-cleared drugs; check BNF
Nephrology (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI stage 2/3 — specialist nephrology input — Intrinsic AKI (e.g. glomerulonephritis) → urgent biopsy consideration
Urology (Urgent (2 wk)): Obstructive AKI — urgent decompression (DJ stent / nephrostomy)
Intensive Care (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI with haemodynamic compromise or hyperkalaemia refractory to medical management → RRT
Nephrology review if no recovery at 48–72h. Repeat U&E at 48h, then weekly until creatinine stable. Avoid nephrotoxins long-term.
Review within 24–48 hours.

Book Emergency Theatre — Acute Diverticulitis

PERFORATED PU:

COLONIC PERFORATION:

management.text: Calculate: NEWS2 — National Early Warning Score 2 — standardised track-and-trigger for physiological deterioration.
Trend CRP vs. prior — Compare current CRP with previous result to assess treatment response / progression.
Draft: SOAP Note — Working diagnosis: Acute Kidney Injury (P=91%) — auto-populate from collected history and exam.
IDENTIFY & TREAT CAUSE:
PRERENAL (commonest — dehydration, sepsis, cardiac output): IV fluid challenge; treat sepsis
INTRINSIC (ATN, nephritis, drugs): stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion)

POSTRENAL (obstruction): urgent renal USS → nephrostomy/stent if hydronephrosis; obstructed infected or solitary kidney → emergency decompression (EAU 2024); bladder outflow obstruction → urethral catheter, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (hourly urine output, replace losses); avoid NSAIDs in AKI
Stop / withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and metformin during AKI; restart when renal function recovers (NICE NG148); urinalysis (dipstick) for every patient with AKI
FLUID MANAGEMENT:
Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, high-output stoma): volume replacement — 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus → reassess response (JVP, UO, BP)
Oliguric AKI (UO <0.5 mL/kg/h): assess volume status; diuretics only for fluid overload, not to treat AKI (NICE NG148)
Fluid overload: fluid restrict ± furosemide; consider dialysis
HYPERKALAEMIA MANAGEMENT:
K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes: calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL) — cardioprotection (UK Kidney Association 2023)

⚠ Mild hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L; 5.5–5.9 — UKKA 2023): potassium-shifting treatment withheld — treat the cause, stop contributing drugs, repeat K⁺ (exclude haemolysis); shifting treatment is for K⁺ ≥ 6.0 mmol/L.
⚠ K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L: nebulised salbutamol withheld — an adjunct for severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.5 mmol/L) only (UKKA 2023).
Kayexalate / patiromer / sodium zirconium (GI elimination)
Restrict dietary K⁺; stop K⁺-sparing drugs
RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) — indications:
Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 despite treatment)
Refractory acidosis (pH <7.1)
Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis
DRUG DOSING: adjust all renally-cleared drugs; check BNF
Nephrology (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI stage 2/3 — specialist nephrology input — Intrinsic AKI (e.g. glomerulonephritis) → urgent biopsy consideration
Urology (Urgent (2 wk)): Obstructive AKI — urgent decompression (DJ stent / nephrostomy)
Intensive Care (Urgent (2 wk)): AKI with haemodynamic compromise or hyperkalaemia refractory to medical management → RRT
Nephrology review if no recovery at 48–72h. Repeat U&E at 48h, then weekly until creatinine stable. Avoid nephrotoxins long-term.
Review within 24–48 hours.

If ≥ 5 mg prednisolone (or equivalent) for > 4 weeks, give steroid cover — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction or at the start of the acute illness, then 200 mg/24 h (infusion, or 50 mg IV/IM 6-hourly) while unwell or nil by mouth, then double the usual oral dose for 48 h (AAGBI/Society for Endocrinology 2020).

[WARNING] VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery (NG89, 2018). management.text: EMERGENCY — Act Now: Sepsis — Initiate 1-Hour Bundle — Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics; IV antibiotics within 1 hour if suspected infection (broad-spectrum; narrow when cultures return); IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 h if lactate ≥4 or hypotension; Vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP <65 despite resuscitation; Measure serum lactate; repeat if initial ≥2 mmol/L; Identify and control source (imaging ± surgical intervention)

EMERGENCY — Act Now: Pulmonary Embolism — ⚠ Lactate 5.2 mmol/L (≥4): Septic shock physiology — target MAP >65, start vasopressors if fluid-unresponsive; ICU/HDU NOW; Oxygen: high-flow if SpO₂ <92% — target SpO₂ 94–98%; IV access + baseline obs; Assess haemodynamic status: SBP <90 mmHg (or a drop >40 mmHg) → massive (high-risk) PE; tachycardia alone is not high-risk (ESC 2019); Massive PE (haemodynamic instability): systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours) is life-saving — contraindicated after major surgery, trauma or bleeding in the previous 3 weeks (surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy instead) (ESC 2019); If sub-massive: anticoagulate and monitor closely; Analgesia for pleuritic pain
Repeat lactate in 2 h — Lactate ≥2 — clearance target ≥10% per hour in sepsis resuscitation.

Suspected pulmonary embolism — two-level Wells score (NICE NG158): Wells > 4 (PE likely) → CTPA directly, with interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed; Wells ≤ 4 → D-dimer, and CTPA only if it is positive. D-dimer is unhelpful after recent surgery and in pregnancy.
HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE (most patients):
DOACs (preferred): rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21d → 20 mg OD; or apixaban 10 mg BD × 7d → 5 mg BD
LMWH (enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg SC OD or 1 mg/kg BD) when a DOAC is unsuitable (renal failure, pregnancy, drug interactions) — no "bridging" to a DOAC
PREGNANCY: anticoagulation with LMWH — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated in pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic) (RCOG GTG 37a/b)
HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE (massive PE — SBP <90):

ADMIT ICU — thrombolysis: alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h — CONTRAINDICATED after major surgery or trauma within 3 weeks, recent stroke or active bleeding (ESC 2019): choose surgical embolectomy / catheter-directed therapy instead
If thrombolysis contraindicated: surgical embolectomy / catheter-directed therapy
Oxygen to a target SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, e.g. COPD) (BTS 2017)
No fluid bolus in suspected PE with RV strain / heart-failure signs — cautious fluids only (ESC 2019)
Duration: provoked → 3 months; unprovoked → ≥6 months; cancer-associated → DOAC long-term
PATIENT-SPECIFIC SAFETY CHECKS (review before acting):

[WARNING] VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89): assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and after surgery (NG89, 2018). Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after surgery if bleeding risk allows, for at least 7 days.
Review 4–6 weeks. Duration decision at 3 months. ECHO if RV dysfunction at index admission.
Urgent surgical review — same day.

management.text: EMERGENCY — Act Now: Incarcerated / Strangulated Hernia — Lactate 2.9 mmol/L: Tissue hypoperfusion — goal-directed IV fluid resuscitation, reassess in 2 h; IV access + prompt fluid resuscitation (up to 30 mL/kg if haemodynamically unstable — SSC 2021); IV analgesia + anti-emetic; NG tube if obstructed (bilious vomiting, distension); Nil by mouth; Attempted manual reduction (taxis) ONLY if: <6 h duration, no peritonism, no systemic compromise — gentle sustained pressure with sedation/analgesia; Do NOT attempt taxis if peritonism, systemic sepsis or suspected ischaemia; Urgent surgical consent for emergency hernia repair

Urgent (< 4 h): Small Bowel Obstruction — Lactate 2.9 mmol/L: Tissue hypoperfusion — goal-directed IV fluid resuscitation, reassess in 2 h; IV access + Hartmann's 1–2 L over 2–4 h (bowel obstruction causes significant third-space loss); Analgesia: morphine IV (reassess regularly); Anti-emetic: metoclopramide or ondansetron IV; NG tube (nasogastric decompression): wide-bore, free drainage + aspirate every hour; IDC for urine output monitoring; Nil by mouth
Book Emergency Theatre — Incarcerated / Strangulated Hernia
Prepare: Operative Note Template — Theatre decision made — pre-populate operative note with diagnosis and planned procedure.
Femoral hernia: prompt (early) repair recommended regardless of symptoms — high strangulation risk (HerniaSurge 2018)
Elective: laparoscopic TEP/TAPP or open repair (low / Lockwood approach; McEvedy / high approach if bowel resection is likely)

Strangulated / obstructed (tender irreducible lump, small bowel obstruction, Richter's): emergency surgery — emergency repair with inspection of bowel viability ± resection; do not attempt reduction if strangulation is suspected (WSES 2017)
Obstructed: nil by mouth, IV fluids, nasogastric (NG) tube decompression and analgesia while theatre is arranged
Obstruction from a hernia is not managed with a water-soluble contrast or conservative trial
Peri-operative (patient-specific):
Fasting: food up to 6 h and clear fluids up to 2 h before anaesthesia (AAGBI 2010; ESA 2011).
Antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose at induction per the local antimicrobial policy (emergency repair; possible contamination); check the allergy record.

investigations.text: U&E / Renal Function — U&E / Renal Function reduces diagnostic uncertainty by 0.1 bits. Strongest discriminator for Acute Ischaemic Stroke (P=64%).
CT Brain (non-contrast) — IMMEDIATE — Exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis; haemorrhage evident immediately
MRI Brain + DWI (diffusion-weighted) — DWI most sensitive for ischaemia within hours — confirms TIA territory
CT/MR Angiography (intracranial + carotid) — Identify large vessel occlusion (LVO) for thrombectomy eligibility
12-lead ECG + cardiac monitoring ≥24h — AF detection — paroxysmal AF in up to 25% of cryptogenic stroke
FBC / Coagulation / U&E / Glucose — Stroke mimics (hypoglycaemia); coagulopathy; anaemia
Lipid profile / HbA1c — Modifiable risk factors
Carotid Doppler Ultrasound — Ipsilateral carotid stenosis >50% → carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks
Echocardiogram (TTE/TOE) — Cardioembolic source — thrombus, PFO, valvular disease
Renal function (creatinine, eGFR / creatinine clearance) — DOAC interruption timing depends on CrCl (PAUSE 2019; BSG/ESGE 2021)

Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm): diagnostic lobectomy (hemithyroidectomy)

Papillary carcinoma with lateral neck nodes (N1b): total thyroidectomy with therapeutic lateral neck dissection (levels II–V) and central compartment dissection

Rapidly enlarging mass with stridor: airway first — anaesthetic and ENT review (awake fibreoptic intubation / tracheostomy planning), urgent core biopsy for anaplastic carcinoma vs lymphoma, urgent MDT
Retrosternal goitre with tracheal compression: total thyroidectomy (cervical approach; sternotomy with cardiothoracic surgery if needed) with anaesthetic airway planning

Mechanical prophylaxis (anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) unless contraindicated (e.g. peripheral arterial disease), plus LMWH — e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily, dose-adjust in renal impairment — CrCl < 30 mL/min: 20 mg once daily (BNF) — from 6–12 h after surgery if bleeding risk allows, for at least 7 days.
Thyroid MDT; ultrasound surveillance for benign nodules.
Routine follow-up as arranged.
